items.prompt: A tester confirms the reset button sends exactly one email per click. Which kind of question did that answer?
choices: Does the feature do what it was built to do?
How could someone misuse the feature on purpose?
Who is allowed to read the email afterwards?
items.explanation: It is a correctness question: the intended use works. It says nothing about misuse.

items.prompt: The security mindset starts from which question?
choices: Does every button on the page respond within a second of being clicked?
What could someone do to this if they wanted to cause harm?
Is the code formatted the same way in every file of the project?
items.explanation: Security asks about deliberate misuse, not speed or style.

items.prompt: A house owner confirms the key opens the front door. Which question is still unasked?
choices: Does the key turn smoothly in the lock?
Is the front door painted a pleasant colour?
Can anyone get in without the key?
items.explanation: The key test covers the intended entry. The unasked question is about unintended entries such as a loose window.

items.prompt: When is threat modeling most useful?
choices: While the design can still change cheaply, before it is built
Only after an attack has already happened to the live system and cost money
Only on launch day, by someone from a different team
items.explanation: Asking early means a missing rule is one extra line, not a redesign.

items.prompt: Which statement is right about a feature whose tests all pass?
choices: No attacker can misuse it, because all of the tests are green
Its intended paths work, but abused paths are unchecked
It is safe as long as the system stays small
items.explanation: Tests check the paths someone imagined. Abuse lives on the paths nobody imagined.

items.prompt: What does the phrase happy path mean?
choices: The route through the code with the fewest security checks on it
The fastest route a request can take through a server
The normal use: one real user doing the expected thing
items.explanation: The happy path is the expected, well-behaved use. Security work targets everything else.

items.prompt: Why do small, little-known sites still get attacked?
choices: Automated scripts try known weaknesses on huge numbers of hosts
Attackers always pick small companies on purpose
Small sites hold more valuable data than large ones
items.explanation: Much real exploitation is untargeted scanning, so being obscure does not make a site invisible.

items.prompt: In one phrase, what is a threat model?
choices: A list of every bug that the tests found during the last release
A look at who might attack and what they want from the system
A diagram of the database tables and how they link to each other
items.explanation: It is a deliberate, early look at attackers, goals and paths, not a bug report.

items.prompt: A team ships a share-link feature after confirming that each link opens the right file. Which review question would have found the biggest gap that testing missed?
choices: Does the link open quickly enough on a slow mobile connection while a large file loads?
What happens if someone alters the link and opens a file that was never shared with them?
Is the link label spelled the same way on every screen?
Does the link still open after the page is refreshed twice?
items.explanation: Only the first asks what a person does who is deliberately trying a link they were not given. The others are quality questions with no adversary in them.
items.reference:
Two different questions about the same feature
🔑 correctness: does the intended use work?
🕵️ security: what can someone do who is trying to misuse it?
passing the first says nothing about the second
Why: tests only walk the paths someone thought of; an adversary walks the others.
items.learnMore:
Correctness is not safety

A test suite lists the uses the author imagined. Threat modeling deliberately imagines the uses nobody intended, ideally while the design can still change cheaply.

Common mistake

Reading a green test run as evidence that nobody can abuse the feature. It only shows the expected paths work.
items.reflection: Think of something you use daily that works perfectly when used as intended. Who might use it in a way its maker never planned?

items.prompt: Two reviewers examine the same checkout form. One asks whether an order with valid inputs completes. The other asks what happens when someone sends inputs the form would never produce. What separates the second reviewer?
choices: Assuming the sender may be deliberate and scripted
Testing the form on more browsers and screen sizes before release
Checking that the same tests pass faster on every build server
Reading the code line by line instead of running it once
items.explanation: The change is one word: the sender is an adversary who can automate and who is not limited to what the interface offers.

items.prompt: A start-up says nobody would bother attacking a product with forty users. Which fact weakens that reasoning the most?
choices: Forty users is below the size at which any attack has been recorded
Attackers prefer targets whose names they have already heard before
Scanners try known weaknesses on huge numbers of hosts without choosing who to target
Tiny systems cannot be patched because they lack the people to do it
items.explanation: Untargeted automation means the question is whether you carry a known weakness, not whether anyone chose you.

items.prompt: A security review is scheduled as a separate gate the week before launch. What is the main weakness of that timing?
choices: Reviewers cannot read code that other teams wrote without a long handover
Late reviews tend to report too many cosmetic problems and too few real ones
Security checks run noticeably slower in production than they do in testing
The design was never examined adversarially, so a fix may mean rework
items.explanation: A missing trust decision is cheap before the design is fixed and expensive after the architecture has been built around it.

items.prompt: A visitor types a value into a web form and it arrives at your server. Is it inside or outside your trust boundary at that moment?
choices: Inside: the form is part of your website
Outside: the visitor controls it
Inside: a real person typed it
items.explanation: Whoever controls the value controls what it says, however friendly the form looks.

items.prompt: The browser sends a field called isAdmin with the value true. What is the safest way to treat it?
choices: As a claim to check against what the server already knows
As a fact, because your own page produced the value in the first place
As a fact, once it has the right data type
items.explanation: A client-supplied value is a claim. The server decides roles from its own records.

items.prompt: Which hop crosses a trust boundary: browser to API, or API to its own database?
choices: API to its own database
Neither one crosses a boundary
Browser to API
items.explanation: The browser is outside your control. The database sits inside what you own.

items.prompt: A webhook arrives claiming to be from a payment provider. What should the server do first?
choices: Trust it because the web address is kept secret
Verify that it really came from that provider
Process it quickly and check later
items.explanation: A claimed sender proves nothing until it is verified, for example with a shared signature.

items.prompt: What does the word trusted mean for data already in your own database?
choices: It did not just arrive from an outside actor
It can never contain a mistake of any kind
No one will ever need to look at it again in the future
items.explanation: Trusted is about where the data came from this moment, not a promise that it is correct forever.

items.prompt: A user uploads a file named photo.jpg. What does the name tell you?
choices: That the file is a real picture
That the file is safe to open
Only what the uploader says
items.explanation: A label is chosen by the uploader. The actual contents have to be checked separately.

items.prompt: In a house, which is outside your trust boundary?
choices: A stranger knocking at the front door
A family member in the kitchen
The lock that you fitted on your own back door yourself
items.explanation: The stranger controls what they say and do. The family member and the lock are things you already know.

items.prompt: Where is re-earning trust most important?
choices: At every line of code in the whole program, equally
Where data crosses into your system
Only inside the database layer, once data is stored
items.explanation: The crossing point is where an outsider can hand you a claim and hope you accept it.

items.prompt: A server takes a request from a browser, writes it to its own database, and later reads that row back to build a page. How many of these three hops come from outside into your control?
choices: Two: the browser request and the database write, since both of them put new data into storage
One: the browser request, since the write and the read stay inside components you own
Three: every hop moves data between two separate components in the system
None: the browser and the server together form a single application that you own
items.explanation: Only the first hop starts with an outside actor. The other two move data between pieces you operate, even though bad data can still travel through them.
items.reference:
Which hop needs re-verifying?
🌐 browser to API: outside actor, claim must be checked
📨 third-party webhook to API: outside actor, sender must be proved
🗄️ API to own database: stays within what you control
Why: trust is re-earned where data crosses from outside into your system, not inherited from its shape.
items.learnMore:
Trust boundaries

A boundary is any place where data passes from something you do not control to something you do. Everything that crosses is a claim, and claims are checked against what the server itself knows.

Common mistake

Treating a well-formed value as a trusted one. A field can have the right type and still be chosen by the attacker.
items.reflection: Pick a place where you hand something to a stranger who then acts on it, such as a delivery note or a form. What do they check before they trust it?

items.prompt: A request says it comes from PayCo and its body says status is paid. Which check addresses the trust boundary?
choices: Checking that the status field holds the exact word paid in lowercase
Checking that the web address is one that few outsiders could guess
Verifying a signature only PayCo and your server can produce
Checking that the body is valid JSON with every expected field filled in
items.explanation: The risk is a forged sender. Only proof of the sender defends against that; content shape and secret-looking addresses do not.

📨 third-party webhook to API: outside actor, sender must be proved

items.prompt: An internal service your API calls is compromised and returns a manipulated value. What does this show about the word trusted?
choices: Trusted only means no outsider is in that hop; a compromised component can still send bad data
Internal services should be avoided by an API because every call adds exposure
Trust boundaries apply only to web browsers and never to services behind the API
Only the database should validate anything, because every other layer can be fooled
items.explanation: Trust is a judgment about where data comes from, not a guarantee. Defence in depth still applies to internal hops.

items.prompt: A form sends role=admin in a hidden field and the server uses it as it arrives. Which statement best explains the failure?
choices: Hidden fields are shown only to developers, so the form should have encrypted the value in the page
The role string was too short for the validator to check it properly before use
The database should have rejected the word admin when the row was written to storage
A value from outside the boundary decided access without being re-derived from server records
items.explanation: Hidden only means not displayed. Anyone can send any value, so access must come from the server's own records.

items.prompt: Which STRIDE letter stands for pretending to be someone else?
choices: S, Spoofing
T, Tampering
E, Elevation of privilege
items.explanation: Spoofing is a forged identity, such as a fake badge.

items.prompt: Which category covers changing a price on its way to the server?
choices: Repudiation
Denial of service
Tampering
items.explanation: Tampering is altering data in transit or at rest.

items.prompt: An admin deletes records and nothing logs who did it. Which category is that?
choices: Spoofing
Repudiation
Information disclosure
items.explanation: With no record, the person can later deny the action, so there is no proof.

items.prompt: An error page shows internal file paths and a stack trace. Which category?
choices: Information disclosure
Tampering
Elevation of privilege
items.explanation: It leaks internal details someone should not see.

items.prompt: Flooding a service so that real users cannot reach it is which category?
choices: Spoofing
Information disclosure
Denial of service
items.explanation: The goal is to make the service unavailable to legitimate use.

items.prompt: A regular user calls an admin-only action that the screen merely hides. Which category?
choices: Information disclosure
Elevation of privilege
Denial of service
items.explanation: They obtain access beyond what was granted. Hiding a button is not a permission check.

items.prompt: What is STRIDE?
choices: Six lenses for asking how a component could be abused
A list of the six most common bugs found in web applications
A tool that scans source code for these problems automatically
items.explanation: It is a set of question categories, not specific bugs or a scanner.

items.prompt: A category clearly does not fit a component, such as repudiation for a profile picture. What do you do?
choices: Invent a threat so every box is filled
Stop the review before the remaining categories
Note low relevance and move on to the others
items.explanation: Not every category applies equally. The point is asking, not filling in every cell.

items.prompt: A customer changes the number in an order address from 118 to 119 and sees a different customer's order. Which STRIDE category names the main harm?
choices: Spoofing, because the order number works as a fake identity
Repudiation, because nothing records who changed the number in the address
Information disclosure, because they read data they should not see
Denial of service, because another order was opened by mistake
items.explanation: The main harm is reading someone else's data. Several lenses can touch one flaw, but the primary harm decides the label.
items.reference:
Six lenses on one component
🎭 Spoofing: pretending to be someone else
✏️ Tampering: altering data or code
🙅 Repudiation: denying an action with no proof
🔓 Information disclosure: reading what you should not
🐘 Denial of service: blocking real users
👑 Elevation of privilege: getting more access than granted
Why: each letter is an independent question, so a clean answer on one says nothing about the other five.
items.learnMore:
STRIDE as lenses, not a bug list

STRIDE names six categories of what could go wrong. You run all six against each component and keep the plausible ones; a category that does not fit can be noted as low relevance and left.

Common mistake

Stopping after one category comes back clean, or inventing a threat just to fill every box.
items.reflection: Choose a shared space such as a library or an office kitchen. Which of the six lenses would reveal the most surprising way it could be misused?

items.prompt: Which pair correctly separates Tampering from Repudiation?
choices: Tampering changes data; repudiation is denying an action when no record proves it
Tampering reads data; repudiation changes data without leaving any trace
Tampering forges a login; repudiation forges a signature
Tampering blocks users from the service; repudiation hides where the attacker connected from
items.explanation: One alters what is stored or sent. The other is about missing evidence of who did what.

items.prompt: An upload endpoint saves each file under the filename the client chose, so two users uploading avatar.png can see each other's picture. Which category and fix fit?
choices: Repudiation; keep a detailed log of every filename that people choose to upload
Information disclosure; store files under a random key scoped to the user
Spoofing; require every person to rename the file before it can be uploaded
Denial of service; allow each person only a single upload in any given hour
items.explanation: The harm is exposure of another user's file. Server-chosen, scoped storage keys remove the collision at its source.

items.prompt: A reviewer finds no repudiation concern for a profile-picture upload and writes that the endpoint is secure. What is wrong with that conclusion?
choices: Repudiation always applies to uploads, so the finding itself must be wrong
Profile pictures are the riskiest component of almost any application
STRIDE should be run once per system, not once for each component
One clear lens says nothing about the other five, each of which needs its own answer
items.explanation: Safe follows only from asking all six questions and getting a clean answer on each.

items.prompt: In threat ranking, what does likelihood mean?
choices: How much damage the attack would cause
How easy or common the attack seems
How long the fix would take to write
items.explanation: Likelihood is about how probable the attack is. Damage is impact.

items.prompt: In threat ranking, what does impact mean?
choices: How much damage it would cause if it happened
How often similar attacks have already been seen elsewhere
How many people on the team know about the problem
items.explanation: Impact is the size of the loss. How often it happens is likelihood.

items.prompt: A threat has likelihood 4 and impact 3. What is its score as likelihood x impact?
items.explanation: 4 x 3 = 12. Adding would give 7, and writing the digits side by side is not arithmetic.

items.prompt: Why rank threats instead of fixing all of them with equal urgency?
choices: Effort is limited, so the largest risks go first
Small risks can safely be ignored forever after the first pass
Ranking removes every risk from the system
items.explanation: Ranking spends limited effort where it matters. It does not make risk vanish.

items.prompt: Which threat ranks higher: likelihood 4 with impact 3, or likelihood 2 with impact 5?
choices: Likelihood 2 with impact 5 (score 10)
Likelihood 4 with impact 3 (score 12)
They tie on score
items.explanation: 12 is larger than 10, so the first one is ranked higher.

items.prompt: Can a threat model remove every possible risk?
choices: Yes, if the model is built carefully enough by the whole team
Yes, once every threat has a score
No; it aims effort at where it matters most
items.explanation: Eliminating all risk is impossible. The aim is a sensible order of work.

items.prompt: After listing what is valuable, what is the next step in a threat model?
choices: List where outside input enters
Write the final fixes
Measure how fast the server responds
items.explanation: You find the entry points, then ask the six STRIDE questions at each.

items.prompt: Which household problem has the highest impact?
choices: A squeaky hinge on the garden gate that nobody uses much
The front door left unlocked while the family is away
A dim bulb on the porch
items.explanation: Impact is about the size of the loss. An unlocked door risks far more than a squeak or a dim bulb.

items.prompt: Four threats are scored likelihood x impact: P is 2 x 4, Q is 3 x 4, R is 4 x 1, S is 5 x 2. Which order is highest score first?
choices: Q, S, P, R
S, R, Q, P
P, Q, S, R
R, P, S, Q
items.explanation: Scores are Q 12, S 10, P 8, R 4. Sorting by likelihood alone or by impact alone gives the other orders.
items.reference:
Rank by likelihood x impact (assumed 1-5 scores)
1. threat: reset link reusable after use, 3 x 4 = 12
2. threat: no rate limit on resend, 5 x 2 = 10
3. threat: guessable token, 1 x 5 = 5
the list sets a starting order, not a final verdict
Why: effort is limited, so ranking decides what gets fixed first without pretending all risk disappears.
items.learnMore:
Ranking threats

After the STRIDE pass you hold a list of plausible threats. Scoring each by how likely it seems and how bad it would be gives a first order; the scores are judgments, so write down the assumptions behind them.

Common mistake

Treating a score as a measurement. A low score with a catastrophic impact and a cheap fix can still deserve early attention.
items.reflection: Think of a list of household repairs you keep postponing. How would you rank them, and which low-ranked one would you still do first?

items.prompt: A threat scores lowest on the list: likelihood 1, impact 5, score 5. A cheap fix exists. What is the sound call?
choices: Ignore it, because its score is the lowest on the whole list
Delay it until a real attack proves that the weakness can be used
Treat the score as a starting order and fix it early, since the fix is cheap
Raise its likelihood score to 5 so that it ranks first on the list and gets fixed
items.explanation: Scores guide, they do not decide. A catastrophic impact with a cheap fix is worth doing regardless of rank.

Rank by likelihood x impact (assumed 1-5 scores)
1. threat: reset link reusable after use, 3 x 4 = 12
2. threat: no rate limit on resend, 5 x 2 = 10
3. threat: guessable token, 1 x 5 = 5
the list sets a starting order, not a final verdict
Why: effort is limited, so ranking decides what gets fixed first without pretending all risk disappears.

Listing every bug that testing has already found in the product
items.explanation: It orders work. It follows a STRIDE pass and does not replace it.

items.explanation: Likelihood and impact are estimates. Surfacing the assumptions behind them is what makes a ranking useful.

The browser, since it displays the price

items.explanation: A value that decides money must come from a source the server owns.

items.prompt: Why does the rule price must be a positive number not stop the bug?
choices: Positive numbers cannot be checked by a server at all
0.01 is a valid positive number; the issue is who chose it
The rule has to run in the browser instead of the server so it works
items.explanation: The format was fine. The failure was letting the client pick the value.

items.prompt: The server takes two items at 19.99 each from its catalog. What is the charge?
The server trusts a tampered request: price 0.01, quantity 2. What is the charge?
items.explanation: 2 x 0.01 = 0.02, so the order is charged two cents.

items.prompt: Which input is reasonable to accept from the client, after limit checks?
choices: The price of each item
How many items to buy
The discount amount to apply
items.explanation: The customer chooses quantity. Price and discounts belong to the shop.

items.prompt: Does the fix change what an honest customer sees?
choices: No: the total is the same, only abused requests differ
Yes: honest customers now pay a higher total than before
Yes: honest customers must enter the price twice
items.explanation: Both versions charge 39.98 for the honest order. The fix only matters under tampering.

items.prompt: Which kind of check shows who chose a value?
choices: Checking that the value is a number and not empty
Checking that it has two decimals
Looking it up in a source the server owns
items.explanation: Shape checks describe the value. Only a server-side source shows it was not chosen by the client.

items.prompt: Where does the trust boundary sit in the checkout bug?
choices: Between the server and its own catalog of products
Between the customer's browser and the server
Between the catalog and the database
items.explanation: The browser is outside your control. The catalog and database are yours.

items.prompt: A teammate adds a rule rejecting prices below 1.00. A customer sends price 18.00 for an item whose catalog price is 19.99. What happens?
choices: The rule rejects it because 18.00 is under the catalog price
The server spots tampering because the price has two decimals
The request fails because the rule is applied to every single price in the catalog
The request passes the rule, and the customer pays less than the catalog price
items.explanation: A minimum only blocks one narrow range. The client still chose the value, so the hole stays open.
items.reference:
Who chose the price?
🧾 vulnerable: price comes from the request, 0.01 x 2 = 0.02 charged
🏪 fixed: price comes from the server catalog, 19.99 x 2 = 39.98 charged
format check: is it a number? trust check: who chose it?
Why: validating the shape of a value never proves the client was allowed to pick it.
items.learnMore:
Re-derive, do not just validate

When a value decides money or access, take it from a source the server owns. Range checks only shrink the set of lies an attacker can tell; they do not remove the lie.

Common mistake

Adding a minimum-price rule. An attacker simply sends a price just above the minimum.
items.reflection: Think of a form you filled in where you supplied a number that the other side should have looked up themselves. What could have gone wrong?

items.prompt: A request carries discount code SAVE10 and a field percentOff set to 90. Which fix follows the same principle as the price fix?
choices: Look up what SAVE10 is worth in the server's own table and ignore the client's number
Reject any percentOff value that is above 50
Cap percentOff at the largest discount any code allows and log every request that exceeds it
Round percentOff to a whole number first
items.explanation: Re-derive the value from server records instead of accepting a number the client supplies.

The boundary moves back one hop: the feed's data must be verified first

items.prompt: Each entry point independently has chance `p` of being exploitable. Implement `chanceNoneFail(p, n)`: the chance that none of `n` entry points fails.
items.explanation: Each entry point stays safe with chance 1 - p, and independent events multiply. With no entry points nothing can fail, so the answer is 1.

items.prompt: Implement `chanceAtLeastOne(p, n)`: the chance that at least one of `n` independent entry points, each failing with chance `p`, is exploitable.
items.explanation: At least one failure is the opposite of none failing, so it is 1 minus the chance that all stay safe.

items.prompt: Implement `expectedFlaws(n, p)`: the average number of exploitable entry points when `n` entry points each have chance `p`.
items.explanation: The average count is n times p. Note this is an average number of flaws, not the chance of having at least one.

items.prompt: Implement `chanceBothFail(p, q)`: the chance two independent entry points both fail, with failure chances `p` and `q`.
items.explanation: Independent events that must both happen multiply their chances.

items.prompt: Implement `chanceEitherFails(p, q)`: the chance at least one of two independent entry points fails, with failure chances `p` and `q`.
items.explanation: Either failing is the opposite of both staying safe. Adding p and q would double count the case where both fail.

items.prompt: Implement `riskPercent(n, perEntryPercent)`. Each of `n` independent entry points has a `perEntryPercent` percent chance of being exploitable. Return the percent chance that at least one is exploitable, rounded to one decimal place.
items.explanation: Convert the percentage to a fraction, compute the chance that none fail, subtract it from 1, and convert back to a percentage rounded to one decimal. Simply multiplying n by the percentage would give 120 percent for 40 entry points.
items.reference:
Risk of at least one exploitable entry point (3% each, independent)
1 entry point: 3.0%
10 entry points: 26.3%
20 entry points: 45.6%
40 entry points: 70.4%
Why: chance of at least one failure is 1 minus the chance that none fail, so it climbs faster than the count of entry points.
items.learnMore:
Why risk is not additive

For independent entry points each with chance p, the chance all stay safe is (1 - p) to the power n. The chance at least one fails is one minus that, which is why 40 small risks are far worse than 40 times one.

Common mistake

Multiplying p by n. That ignores overlap and goes past 100% for large n.
items.reflection: Think of a chain of small things that each usually go right, like a morning routine. How does the chance that everything goes right change as you add steps?

items.prompt: Implement `entryPointsToReach(targetPercent, perEntryPercent)`: the smallest number of independent entry points, each with a `perEntryPercent` percent chance of being exploitable, for which the chance of at least one exploitable entry point reaches `targetPercent`.
items.explanation: Risk grows with each added entry point, so counting upward until the chance reaches the target finds the smallest n. Dividing the target by the per-entry chance assumes risks add, which badly overcounts how many are needed.

Why: chance of at least one failure is 1 minus the chance that none fail, so it climbs faster than the count of entry points.

items.prompt: Implement `riskAfterRetiring(n, retired, perEntryPercent)`: a system has `n` independent entry points, each with a `perEntryPercent` percent chance of being exploitable. After `retired` of them are removed, return the percent chance at least one remaining entry point is exploitable, rounded to one decimal place.
items.explanation: Only the remaining entry points can fail, so recompute the at-least-one chance for n minus retired. Halving the count does not halve the risk: 40 entry points are about 70.4 percent, 20 are about 45.6 percent.
